title: Difference between Section 41 credit and Section 174 expenses
description: Section 174/174A sets when research costs are deducted or amortized; the Section 41 credit cuts tax directly, and Section 280C(c) bars double benefits.
summary: Section 174 (and, for domestic costs from 2025, Section 174A) is a cost-recovery rule that sets when U.S. businesses deduct or amortize research and experimental expenditures, while the Section 41 research credit directly reduces federal tax liability based on a narrower subset of domestic qualified research expenses; Section 280C(c) prevents claiming both full benefits on the same dollars.

body.text: Section 174 (and, for domestic costs from 2025, Section 174A) is a cost-recovery rule that sets when U.S. businesses deduct or amortize research and experimental expenditures, while the Section 41 research credit directly reduces federal tax liability based on a narrower subset of domestic qualified research expenses; Section 280C(c) prevents claiming both full benefits on the same dollars.

Status of law reflected: Internal Revenue Code as amended by Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025), Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Notices 2023-63 and 2024-12, Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 and December 2025) and its Official Instructions, and IRS release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025). Prepared November 11, 2026. This report is informational and is not legal or tax advice.
1. Summary: Two Provisions, Two Different Jobs

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 (and, for domestic research or experimental costs paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, IRC Section 174A) is a cost-recovery and timing rule: it dictates when and how research or experimental (R&E) expenditures are deducted or amortized in computing taxable income. By contrast, IRC Section 41 is a tax credit: it directly reduces federal income tax liability (or, for eligible startups making a valid election under Section 41(h), payroll tax liability) by a statutory percentage of a much narrower, strictly filtered subset of domestic research costs known as qualified research expenses (QREs).
The two provisions operate in tandem and are legally linked in three primary ways:

items: Threshold Eligibility Link: Section 41 qualified research must first constitute research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(b)(1)).

Geographic Split: Section 41 strictly excludes foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States (§ 41(d)(4)(F)), whereas Section 174 defines and governs the foreign R&E expenditure pool and mandates 15-year capitalization and amortization for foreign research (§ 174(a)–(b)).

Anti-Double-Benefit Coordination: Section 280C(c) prevents a taxpayer from claiming both an unreduced Section 174A deduction (or capital account charge) and a full Section 41 research credit for the exact same expenditure dollars.

cells: Determines timing of deduction: current deduction for domestic R&E (§ 174A(a)) or optional capitalization and amortization over at least 60 months (§ 174A(c)); mandatory 15-year capitalization and amortization for foreign R&E (§ 174(a)).

Provides a dollar-for-dollar credit against tax liability: 20% of QREs over a base amount under the regular credit (§ 41(a)(1)) or 14% (or 6% where no prior-three-year QREs exist) under the alternative simplified credit (§ 41(c)(4)).
Applies to qualifying expenditures by operation of law; taxpayers must properly classify and account for R&E costs under § 174 and § 174A.
Elective benefit claimed by the taxpayer on Form 6765; claiming the credit is optional, though underlying cost classification under § 174/174A is mandatory.
Covers both domestic research (§ 174A) and foreign research (§ 174, subject to mandatory 15-year amortization).
Strictly domestic: research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions is excluded (§ 41(d)(4)(F)).

Broad: includes direct wages, supplies, allocable facility overhead (rent, utilities, insurance, depreciation), patent procurement and perfection costs, and all software development costs (§ 174(c)(3); § 174A(b); Notice 2023-63).

Narrow: limited strictly to in-house wages for qualified services, supplies used in qualified research, amounts paid or incurred for the right to use computers in qualified research, and 65% (or 75%/100% for specific consortia/energy research) of contract research expenses (§ 41(b)).

Costs must represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense" aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a); Notice 2023-63, sec. 2.01(2)).

Must satisfy all four statutory tests: (1) the Section 174A eligibility test, (2) the discovering-technological-information test, (3) the business-component test, and (4) the process-of-experimentation test (§ 41(d)(1); IRS Audit Techniques Guide).
Establishes the broader baseline pool of research or experimental expenditures.

Represents a narrower subset of the domestic R&E pool; § 280C(c) reduces the § 174A deduction (or capital charge) by the full § 41(a) credit claimed unless the taxpayer timely elects the reduced credit under § 280C(c)(2).

body.text: 2. Section 174: How Research Expenditures Are Recovered
2.1 Before 2022

Before the amendments enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) took effect, taxpayers could elect to currently deduct research or experimental expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred under former § 174(a), or elect to amortize them over a period of not less than 60 months under former § 174(b). The TCJA amendments were enacted in December 2017 with a delayed effective date applying to amounts "paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021" (statutory effective-date note to 26 U.S.C. § 174), confirming that the mandatory capitalization regime began with the 2022 taxable year for calendar-year taxpayers.
2.2 Mandatory Capitalization: Tax Years Beginning 2022 Through 2024

items: 5-Year Domestic and 15-Year Foreign Amortization: Under the TCJA version of 26 U.S.C. § 174, taxpayers were required to charge specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures to capital account and amortize them ratably over a 5-year period for domestic research and a 15-year period for foreign research, with amortization beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures were paid or incurred (§ 174(a)(2)(B)).

First-Year Midpoint Convention (10% Domestic / 3.33% Foreign): Because amortization commences at the midpoint of the first taxable year, a calendar-year taxpayer's Year 1 amortization deduction for domestic SRE expenditures was exactly half of one-fifth, or 10% of the capitalized expenditure (1/5 × 1/2 = 10%), followed by 20% in Years 2 through 5 and the remaining 10% in Year 6. For foreign SRE expenditures, the first-year deduction was half of one-fifteenth, or 3.33% (1/15 × 1/2).

Mandatory Inclusion of Software Development: Under § 174(c)(3), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software is statutorily treated as a research or experimental expenditure. Consequently, mandatory capitalization reached all businesses incurring software development costs, regardless of whether those taxpayers ever claimed or qualified for the Section 41 research credit.

Disposition, Retirement, or Abandonment Rule: Under § 174(d), if any property with respect to which specified research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the amortization period, no deduction is allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the taxpayer must continue to amortize the unrecovered basis over the remainder of the statutory amortization period.

body.text: 2.3 Section 174A: Domestic Expensing From 2025

items: Enactment of Public Law 119-21: Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, commonly referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or Working Families Tax Cuts) was signed into law on July 4, 2025. Section 70302 of Pub. L. 119-21 added new IRC Section 174A ("Temporary or Permanent Rules for Domestic Research and Experimental Expenditures" codified as permanent law under 26 U.S.C. § 174A) and amended IRC Section 174.

Immediate Deduction or Elective Amortization for Domestic R&E: Under new § 174A(a), taxpayers may currently deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Alternatively, under § 174A(c), a taxpayer may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures to capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures.

Permanent Statutory Enactment: Unlike several individual and temporary business tax provisions in Pub. L. 119-21 that carry explicit sunset dates (such as 2028 expiration dates for certain deductions), Section 70302 of Pub. L. 119-21 enacted IRC § 174A on a permanent basis for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, with no statutory sunset date.

Continued 15-Year Amortization for Foreign R&E: Foreign research or experimental expenditures (research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States) remain governed by amended § 174(a)–(b). They cannot be deducted currently and must continue to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which paid or incurred.

Tightened Disposition Rule for Foreign R&E Property: For foreign R&E property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, amended § 174(d) provides that no deduction is allowed with respect to such expenditures on account of the disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and no reduction to the amount realized is permitted upon disposition; amortization must continue over the remainder of the 15-year period.

body.text: 2.4 Transition Rules for 2022–2024 Capitalized Domestic Costs

items: Unamortized 2022–2024 Balance Recovery (1-Year or 2-Year Acceleration): Under Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(f)(2) (codified as a statutory transition note to 26 U.S.C. § 174A) and detailed in IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28, any taxpayer that capitalized domestic SRE expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized domestic balance either (i) entirely in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or (ii) ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. This transition change is implemented on a cut-off basis with no § 481(a) adjustment required.

Small Business Retroactive Election Scope and Threshold: Under Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(f)(1) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an eligible small business taxpayer is any taxpayer (other than a tax shelter prohibited from using the cash method under § 448(a)(3)) that meets the § 448(c) average annual gross receipts test for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024—meaning average annual gross receipts for the three prior taxable years of $31,000,000 or less (the inflation-adjusted § 448(c) threshold for taxable years beginning in 2025). Furthermore, the retroactive election applies to all taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, which for calendar-year taxpayers covers 2022, 2023, and 2024 (not merely 2022 and 2023). Under the statute and Rev. Proc. 2025-28, this election must be made within one year of the July 4, 2025 enactment date (by July 6, 2026, accounting for the weekend/holiday rule under § 7503) and requires filing amended federal income tax returns (or administrative adjustment requests for BBA partnerships) for each affected taxable year.

Accounting Method Change Mechanics: Under Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(e)–(f) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28, transitioning to current domestic expensing under § 174A(a) (or elective amortization under § 174A(c)) for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, is treated by statute as a change in method of accounting initiated by the taxpayer and made with the automatic consent of the Secretary of the Treasury on a cut-off basis. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 waives the requirement to file a separate Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) for taxpayers that simply deduct their 2025 domestic R&E expenditures under § 174A(a) on their timely filed 2025 federal income tax return, deeming compliance on the return itself to satisfy the method change requirement, while providing optional streamlined statement procedures for taxpayers recovering unamortized 2022–2024 costs over one or two years.

body.text: 3. Section 41: The Narrower Credit
3.1 Who and What Qualifies (The Statutory Four-Part Test)
Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), in order for activities to constitute "qualified research" eligible for the research tax credit, the research must satisfy four cumulative statutory requirements:

items: The Section 174A Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)): The research must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (as updated by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(b)(1) to cross-reference § 174A rather than § 174).

The Technological-in-Nature Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature—meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)).

The Business-Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & § 41(d)(2)–(3)): The application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer). Under § 41(d)(3)(A), the research must be undertaken for a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality—and under § 41(d)(3)(B) cannot relate to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

The Process-of-Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more) of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

body.text: Framing of the Four-Part Test: As codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and stated in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Activities, the four statutory tests are: (1) the Section 174/174A test, (2) discovering technological information, (3) business component, and (4) process of experimentation. The elimination of technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design is an integral threshold element embedded within both the Section 174/174A test (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)) and the process-of-experimentation test (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)), rather than a standalone statutory test that replaces the Section 174A threshold requirement.
3.2 Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)

items: Statutory Structure: Under § 41(b)(1), total qualified research expenses equal the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer.
In-House Research Expenses (§ 41(b)(2)(A)): In-house research expenses consist strictly of three statutory categories:

Any wages (as defined in § 3401(a), or self-employment earned income under § 401(c)(2)) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee—specifically, engaging in qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(B)). Under the "substantially all" rule of § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an employee's services during the taxable year consist of qualified services, 100% of that employee's wages qualify as QREs.

Any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)). Under § 41(b)(2)(C), the term "supplies" means any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation.

Under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(iii); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)), which in modern practice includes cloud computing server hosting costs used directly for development and testing environments (excluding general business hosting).

Contract Research Expenses (§ 41(b)(3)): Contract research expenses are generally limited to 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research. Higher statutory percentages apply exclusively to payments to qualified research consortia (75% under § 41(b)(3)(C)) and payments for eligible energy research conducted by universities, federal laboratories, or eligible small businesses (100% under § 41(b)(3)(D)).

body.text: 3.3 Why Every QRE Is an R&E Expenditure, But Not the Reverse

Because § 41(d)(1)(A) mandates that qualified research must first be research whose costs are eligible to be treated as domestic R&E expenditures under § 174A, the domestic R&E pool is the mandatory outer boundary and starting point for all QREs. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide emphasizes, Section 41 is substantially more restrictive than Section 174/174A. Major categories of costs that sit inside the § 174/174A R&E pool but are excluded from § 41 QREs include:

items: Foreign Research Expenditures: Research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions falls into § 174's mandatory 15-year amortization pool (§ 174(a)–(b)) and is statutorily barred from § 41 by § 41(d)(4)(F).

Patent Procurement and Legal Costs: Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and Notice 2023-63, sec. 4.03(1)(d), the costs of obtaining a patent—including attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application—are expressly included in R&E / SRE expenditures. Conversely, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3) confirm that patent application legal fees do not qualify for the § 41 credit.

Allocable Facility Overhead and Depreciation: Under Notice 2023-63, sec. 4.03, rent, utilities, insurance, security, taxes, repair and maintenance costs, and depreciation or amortization allowances are included in R&E expenditures to the extent allocable to research activities. However, § 41(b) strictly omits overhead and general and administrative costs, and § 41(b)(2)(C) explicitly excludes depreciable property from qualifying as supplies.

Software Development Failing the § 41(d) Four-Part Test or High-Threshold-of-Innovation Test: While § 174(c)(3) sweeps all software development costs into the § 174 / § 174A framework, software development generates QREs under § 41 only if the activities satisfy the four-part test of § 41(d)(1) (and, for internal-use software under § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), the additional three-part "high threshold of innovation" test requiring that the software be innovative, involve significant economic risk, and not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer).

Post-Research Quality Control, Routine Testing, Market Research, and Funded Research: Section 41(d)(4) expressly excludes research after commercial production (§ 41(d)(4)(A)), adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), duplication of an existing business component (§ 41(d)(4)(C)), surveys, routine data collection, market research, and routine quality control testing (§ 41(d)(4)(D)), research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (§ 41(d)(4)(G)), and research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity (§ 41(d)(4)(H)).

body.text: 3.4 Credit Rates and the Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Election

items: Regular Credit vs. Alternative Simplified Credit Rates: The Internal Revenue Code provides two distinct calculation methods on Form 6765:

The Regular Research Credit (§ 41(a)(1) & § 41(c)): Equals 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's current-year QREs over a statutory "base amount" calculated using the taxpayer's historical fixed-base percentage (ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for 1984–1988, or the startup fixed-base percentage rules under § 41(c)(3)(B) starting at 3% for the first five qualifying years and adjusting thereafter, capped at a maximum fixed-base percentage of 16%) multiplied by the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years (subject to a minimum base amount of 50% of current-year QREs under § 41(c)(2)).

The Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) (§ 41(c)(4)): Equals 14% of so much of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (§ 41(c)(4)(A)). Under § 41(c)(4)(B), if the taxpayer has no qualified research expenses in any one of the three preceding taxable years, the credit rate is 6% of current-year QREs (with no base amount subtraction). Thus, the 6% ASC rate is triggered strictly by the absence of QREs in at least one of the three prior taxable years—not by how many years the taxpayer has previously filed a credit claim.

Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit Election (§ 41(h)): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h), a "qualified small business" (defined under § 41(h)(3) as a corporation, partnership, or individual with gross receipts of less than $5,000,000 for the current taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with the current taxable year) may elect on Form 6765 (Section D) and Form 8974 to apply a portion of its research credit against the employer share of Social Security (OASDI) and Medicare payroll taxes. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022 (as enhanced by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, Pub. L. 117-169, § 13902), the annual payroll tax credit election cap is $500,000 ($250,000 against the 6.2% OASDI tax under § 3111(a) plus up to an additional $250,000 against the 1.45% Hospital Insurance/Medicare tax under § 3111(b)). A taxpayer may not make this election if it has already made a payroll tax credit election for five or more preceding taxable years (§ 41(h)(4)(B)(ii)). Unused general business research credits under § 41 carry back 1 year and carry forward up to 20 years under 26 U.S.C. § 39(a)(1), whereas unused payroll tax credits elected under § 41(h) carry forward to succeeding calendar quarters on Form 941.

body.text: 4. Section 280C(c): The Anti-Double-Benefit Rule
4.1 Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2024
As amended by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(b)(2)(B), 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) restores the traditional dollar-for-dollar deduction reduction rule to coordinate with immediate domestic expensing under § 174A:

items: Default Rule (§ 280C(c)(1)): Any domestic research or experimental expenditures otherwise taken into account as a current deduction under § 174A(a) or charged to capital account under § 174A(c) must be reduced by the full amount of the research credit determined under § 41(a) for the taxable year.

Reduced Credit Election (§ 280C(c)(2)): To avoid reducing its § 174A deduction (and to simplify state tax return conformity or financial statement tax accounting), a taxpayer may elect on a timely filed original return (including extensions) to claim a reduced Section 41 credit. Under § 280C(c)(2)(B), the reduced credit equals the full § 41(a) credit minus the product of that credit multiplied by the maximum corporate income tax rate under 26 U.S.C. § 11(b) (currently 21%). Thus, a taxpayer electing § 280C(c)(2) retains 100% of its § 174A deduction and receives 79% of the gross § 41 research credit (100% − 21% = 79%). Once made for a taxable year, the election is irrevocable.

body.text: 4.2 Tax Years Beginning 2022 Through 2024

During the 2022–2024 mandatory capitalization window under the TCJA version of § 280C(c)(1), the capital account reduction operated differently: the amount chargeable to the § 174 capital account was reduced only to the extent that the § 41(a)(1) research credit exceeded the amount allowable as an amortization deduction for those qualified research expenses for the taxable year. Because the first-year domestic amortization deduction was 10% of the expenditure while the net research credit was typically 6% to 10% of QREs, the credit rarely exceeded the amortization deduction in Year 1, though many taxpayers still elected the § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit out of caution or state-tax conformity considerations.
4.3 Transition Coordination Under Rev. Proc. 2025-28

When an eligible small business taxpayer elects under Pub. L. 119-21 § 70302(f)(1) to apply § 174A domestic expensing retroactively to taxable years 2022, 2023, and 2024, the amended § 280C(c)(1) full deduction-reduction rule applies retroactively to those years as well. Recognizing that taxpayers may have made (or foregone) a § 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election under the prior 2022–2024 capitalization rules that is no longer optimal once 100% domestic expensing is applied retroactively, IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 grants relief: an eligible small business taxpayer applying retroactive § 174A expensing may make a late § 280C(c)(2) election, or revoke a previously made § 280C(c)(2) election, for any eligible prior taxable year (whose original return was filed on or before September 15, 2025) by filing an amended return (or AAR) on or before July 6, 2026.
4.4 Hypothetical Worked Example (2025 Tax Year, C Corporation)
Hypothetical facts: A calendar-year U.S. C corporation incurs $900,000 of total domestic research and experimental expenditures in 2025, consisting of:

items: $500,000 of in-house employee wages for software engineers whose activities satisfy all four tests of § 41(d)(1);
$50,000 of non-depreciable tangible supplies consumed directly in qualified research testing;
$100,000 paid to an unrelated U.S.-based contractor for qualified engineering research where the taxpayer bears the financial risk and retains substantial rights;
$200,000 of allocable R&D laboratory facility rent, utilities, and equipment depreciation; and
$50,000 of outside patent attorneys' fees for preparing and prosecuting patent applications.

body.text: The corporation's average annual QREs for the three preceding taxable years (2022–2024) were $400,000, and the corporation calculates its research credit using the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under § 41(c)(4).

cells: $500,000 (wages) + $50,000 (supplies) + $65,000 (65% × $100,000 contract research); facility overhead/depreciation ($200,000) and patent fees ($50,000) excluded

body.text: Analytical takeaway: As demonstrated in the table above, $285,000 of the corporation's $900,000 domestic research spend ($200,000 of facility overhead and depreciation, $50,000 of patent prosecution fees, and the 35% statutory haircut of $35,000 on contract research) is 100% deductible under § 174A(a) but excluded from § 41 QREs. Moreover, for a C corporation taxed at the flat 21% federal rate under § 11(b), Option A and Option B yield the exact same net federal tax benefit ($58,100 credit − ($58,100 × 21% lost tax deduction) = $45,899 net benefit), whereas for pass-through owners in higher individual income tax brackets (up to 37% under § 1) or taxpayers in states that conform to federal taxable income without a state-level § 280C deduction addback, electing the reduced credit under Option B is often mathematically superior.
5. Contract and Funded Research: "Substantial Rights" vs. "Right to Exploit"
One of the sharpest divergences between Section 41 and Section 174/174A arises when research is performed under contract between a customer (research recipient) and a contractor (research provider):

items: Section 41 Funded Research Rule ("Economic Risk" and "Substantial Rights"): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), research performed by a taxpayer on behalf of another person or governmental entity is disqualified as "funded research" unless the contractor satisfies a strict conjunctive two-prong test:

Contingent Payment (Economic Risk): Amounts payable under the agreement must be contingent on the success of the research (meaning the contractor bears the financial risk of failure; see Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)); and

Substantial Rights: The performer must retain "substantial rights" in the research results (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3); see Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)). Incidental rights or rights to use general know-how only upon paying a royalty do not constitute substantial rights. If either prong fails, the research is treated as funded to the performer, barring the performer from claiming the § 41 credit. Conversely, from the customer's perspective under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is a qualifying contract research expense only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, requires the research to be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful.

Section 174 / 174A Contract Research Framework (Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12): In Notice 2023-63 (issued September 8, 2023, sec. 6), the Treasury Department and the IRS established a distinct test for determining when a contract research provider incurs SRE expenditures under § 174:
Financial Risk Test: If the research provider bears financial risk under the terms of the contract (i.e., payment is contingent on the success of the research), its costs are SRE expenditures.

Right to Exploit Test: Even if the research provider bears no financial risk (for example, under a time-and-materials or cost-plus contract where it cannot claim a § 41 credit because the research is funded), Notice 2023-63, sec. 6.04 provides that the provider must still treat its costs as SRE expenditures if the provider has a right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit any resulting SRE product through sale, lease, or license. However, a right is not treated as an SRE product right if the provider must obtain the approval of an unrelated party to the contract before exploiting the product.

Clarification in Notice 2024-12 ("Excluded SRE Product Right"): Following taxpayer feedback that standard service contracts often grant contractors routine rights to use background tools or contract deliverables purely to service the client, the IRS issued Notice 2024-12 (effective retroactively to September 8, 2023). Section 3 of Notice 2024-12 modifies Notice 2023-63 by creating an exception for an "excluded SRE product right"—defined as an SRE product right that (a) is separately bargained for (resulting in consideration independent of the SRE activities), or (b) was acquired for the limited purpose of performing SRE activities under that contract or another contract with the research recipient. If a non-risk-bearing contractor holds only an excluded SRE product right and no other right to exploit the underlying SRE product, its costs are ordinary business costs under § 162 rather than § 174/174A R&E expenditures.

Explicit Separation of Regimes: Notice 2023-63, sec. 1 explicitly states that the guidance provided therein "is not intended to change the rules for determining eligibility for or computation of the research credit under § 41 and the regulations thereunder." Consequently, the exact same contract can result in different treatment under § 41 versus § 174/174A.

body.text: 6. Reporting and Substantiation: Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 and December 2025)

The IRS comprehensively redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) beginning with the December 2024 revision and further updated in the December 2025 revision and IRS News Release IR-2025-99 (issued October 1, 2025).

items: Phase-In Timeline for Section G: In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) and the official Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), the IRS extended the transition period: Section G (Business Component Information) remains optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026). Section G becomes mandatory beginning with tax year 2026 (taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026), subject to two permanent exemptions under which completing Section G remains optional:
Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit Filers: Taxpayers that are qualified small businesses under § 41(h)(3) and check the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit; and

Small QRE Filers on Original Returns: Taxpayers with total qualified research expenses of $1,500,000 or less (determined at the controlled-group level) and gross receipts of $50,000,000 or less (determined under § 448(c)(3) at the controlled-group level), provided they are claiming the research credit on a timely filed original return.
Structure of New Sections E, F, and G on Form 6765:

Section E — Other Information (Lines 37–41, Mandatory Beginning Tax Year 2024): Every taxpayer claiming a research credit (reporting positive QREs in Section F, line 48) must complete Section E, which requires five specific disclosures:
Line 37: Enter the total number of business components generating the QREs reported on line 5 or line 20 (and line 48).
Line 38: Enter the dollar amount of corporate officers' wages included in total wage QREs on line 42 (with "officer" determined under the laws of the state in which the corporation is incorporated).

Line 39: Indicate (Yes/No) whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business during the tax year (triggering the consistency and base-period adjustment rules of § 41(f)(3)).
Line 40: Indicate (Yes/No) whether the taxpayer identified any new categories of expenditures included as current-year QREs that were not included in prior baseline years.

Line 41: Indicate (Yes/No) whether any portion of the QREs claimed on the return was determined under the IRS Large Business & International (LB&I) ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Directive (which permits qualifying LB&I taxpayers with audited U.S. GAAP financial statements to compute safe-harbor QREs starting from financial statement ASC 730 R&D expense).

Section F — Qualified Research Expenses Summary (Lines 42–48, Mandatory Beginning Tax Year 2024): Centralizes the aggregate QRE breakdown by category that previously appeared inside Sections A and B: Line 42 (Total qualified wages), Line 43 (Total cost of supplies), Line 44 (Total rental or lease cost of computers), Line 45 (Total applicable percentage of contract research expenses), Line 46 (Basic research payments to qualified organizations under § 41(e)), and Line 48 (Total QREs carried to Section A or Section B).

Section G — Business Component Information (Lines 49–56, Optional for Tax Years 2024–2025; Mandatory Starting Tax Year 2026 Unless Exempt): Requires taxpayers to report granular project-level data for their top business components that account for at least 80% of total QREs, capped at a maximum of 50 business components displayed directly on Section G (with the remaining business components aggregated on an "Aggregate" line). For each reported business component, the taxpayer must provide: (a) the EIN of the controlled group member conducting the research, (b) the principal business activity code, (c) the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier, (d) the business component type (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention), (e) for software business components, the software classification (Internal Use Software [IUS], Dual Function Software [DFS], Non-IUS, or Excepted from IUS treatment), and (f) a disaggregated breakdown of QREs for that specific business component across direct research wages (Line 50), direct supervision wages (Line 51), direct support wages (Line 52), total wages (Line 53), supplies (Line 54), computer rental/lease costs (Line 55), and applicable contract research expenses (Line 56).

Substantiation Standards for Amended Return Refund Claims and Judicial Precedent: For taxpayers claiming a Section 41 credit on an amended return or administrative adjustment request (such as small businesses amending 2022–2024 returns under Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and adjusting their credit positions), the IRS enforces the five-item administrative specificity threshold originally announced in Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F (with the IRS transition period extended while eliminating the fourth and fifth items in June 2024 so that refund claimants must provide with the amended claim: (1) all business components to which the § 41 research credit claim relates for that year, (2) for each business component, all research activities performed, and (3) the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year, which may be satisfied by properly completing Form 6765). Furthermore, recent federal appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence—most notably Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, and Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37—confirms that arbitrary, unsubstantiated high-level percentage allocations fails the "substantially all" (80%) process-of-experimentation requirement of § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous project-level documentation linking employee activities and costs to specific business components.

body.text: 7. Classifying Costs in Practice (Three-Bucket Operational Framework)

To comply simultaneously with IRC Section 174/174A and IRC Section 41 without overstating the tax credit or understating mandatory R&E classifications, tax accounting practice divides technical and engineering workflows into three distinct tracking buckets at the chart-of-accounts and time-tracking level:

items: Bucket 1 — Non-R&E Ordinary Business Expenses (§ 162): Routine post-production maintenance, bug fixes that do not improve functionality, routine quality control testing, customer support, employee training, market research, general and administrative overhead unrelated to R&D, and software implementation or data conversion activities excluded under Notice 2023-63, sec. 5.03. These costs are deducted currently under § 162 and never enter the § 174/174A or § 41 computations.

Bucket 2 — Section 174 / 174A R&E Expenditures Only (Excluded From § 41 QREs): Costs that satisfy the broad "experimental or laboratory sense" definition of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 or the statutory software development inclusion of § 174(c)(3), but fail one or more filters of § 41. This bucket includes:
Foreign R&D costs (subject to mandatory 15-year capitalization and amortization under § 174(a));

Domestic allocable R&D facility overhead (rent, utilities, property insurance, depreciation of research equipment) and patent application legal fees (deductible currently under § 174A(a) for 2025+, but excluded from § 41(b));
The non-creditable 35% portion of domestic contract research expenses;

Contract research costs incurred by a service provider that lacks substantial rights or economic risk under § 41(d)(4)(H) but retains a non-excluded right to exploit the SRE product under Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12; and

Domestic software development activities (such as planning, design, coding, and testing prior to commercial readiness under Notice 2023-63, sec. 5.02) that do not resolve technical uncertainty through a formal process of experimentation or fail the high-threshold-of-innovation test for internal-use software under § 41(d)(4)(E).

Bucket 3 — Dual-Qualifying Domestic Costs (§ 174A R&E Expenditures AND § 41 QREs): Domestic in-house wages (direct research, direct supervision, direct support), non-depreciable tangible supplies, leased computer/cloud development server costs, and 65% (or 75%/100%) of domestic contract research expenses incurred in activities that satisfy all four prongs of the § 41(d)(1) test for a specific business component. These costs are included in the § 174A domestic deduction pool (subject to § 280C(c) coordination) and reported by business component on Form 6765 to generate the Section 41 tax credit.
